d.x: Ew! There’s a fly in my soup.

d.g: To express disgust (at someone or something) by saying ew.
d.x: “Brad went into a seething rage, as you do,” said Jack “and followed Harvey out of the restaurant, down the road and …” / “… Killed him with a muttonbird,” added Matahina / “A brick, then a muttonbird,” corrected Jack, to her horror. / “Ew!” she ewwed.

d.g: A female sheep, as opposed to a ram.
d.x: This twentie yeeres haue I bene with thee: thy ewes and thy ſhee goates haue not caſt their yong, and the rammes of thy flocke haue I not eaten.

ewe.e: From Middle English ewe, from Old English eowu, from Proto-West Germanic *awi, from Proto-Germanic *awiz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ówis (“sheep”). Cognates See also Old English ēow (“sheep”), West Frisian ei, Dutch ooi, German Aue; also Old Irish oí, Latin ovis, Tocharian B ā(ᵤ)w, Lithuanian avi̇̀s (“ewe”), Russian овца́ (ovcá).

d.g: a member of the people inhabiting an area of northern Mongolia and eastern Siberia
A kind of widemouthed pitcher or jug with a shape like a vase and a handle, and originally used for carrying water.

ewer.e: From Middle English ewer, from Anglo-Norman or Old French ewer, eawer (modern French évier), from Latin aquārium, from aqua (“water”). Doublet of aquarium.

d.g: A malignant small-round-blue-cell tumor that forms in bone or soft tissue.

Ewing's sarcoma.e: First described by James Ewing (1866–1943), American pathologist.

d.g: Cyberspace and its penetration into the nonvirtual world.
An orogastric tube used to pump the stomach.

Ewald tube.e: Named after the German gastroenterologist Carl Anton Ewald.

d.g: A poor person's sole possession (in reference to the Bible, 2 Samuel xii).
d.x: It was my first book, my only book, my ewe lamb; but it was not a “work,” not an “important publication, ” like Mr. Lecky's “Map of Life." The reviewers did not welcome it either eagerly or seriously.

ewe lamb.e: From Middle English ewe lambren pl.

d.g: A type of below-the-knee amputation, which reconstructs agonist-antagonist myoneural interfaces that are left hanging unpaired in traditional amputations; to preserve normal nerve signaling between muscle and brain; reducing incidences of phantom limb syndrome.
similar amputations above the knee, and on the arms.

Ewing amputation.e: Ewing+amputation. Named after the first patient treated with this type of amputation, Jim Ewing.

d.x: “Ew!” she hissed. “I think what you do is ewwy!”

d.g: A village and civil parish (served by Ewyas Harold Group Parish Council) in the Golden Valley, western Herefordshire, England (OS grid ref SO3828).

Ewyas Harold.e: Recorded as Euwias c.1150, and Euuiasharold in 1176, with the Harold affix coming from a nobleman. Ewyas (cf.) was supposed to be a Welsh kingdom, and this area was originally in Wales.
